word_order: SVO | Subjects precede verbs and verbs precede objects in main clauses in the sample (e.g., 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device', 'Mutations can have a variety of effects').
register: formal written expository prose (news reports / encyclopedia / technical description)
discourse_markers: subordinating conjunctions that introduce dependent clauses (although, because)
coordinating conjunctions that link clauses or clauses-in-progress (and, but)
temporal/relational prepositional openers used as discourse links (after, prior to)
clause_boundary_signals: complementizers / clause introducers marking content clauses (that)
relative pronouns and relative constructions that attach to nouns and open relative clauses (which, who/that)
subordinating conjunctions introducing adverbial clauses (if, once, while)
non-finite clause markers (present-participial -ing clauses, infinitival to) that form subordinate clauses
non_boundary_traps: sentence-initial prepositional or temporal adjuncts that look like opens but attach to the following clause (for over a thousand years, around 60 cases)
comma-set parentheticals and appositives that interrupt flow but do not end clauses (live on television, of course)
possessive / genitive markers that separate words but do not signal clause breaks (Auckland's)
unstable_prefix_signals: subordinating conjunctions and clause introducers that leave the upcoming relation unresolved (although, because, if, while)
sentence-initial adverbial/prepositional phrases and quantifiers whose scope can be revised by the following clause (for over..., around 60, only)
determiners and numerals that require the following nominal to fix reference (the, a, eighteen percent)
notes_for_prompt_writer: Main clauses in the sample are canonical English SVO; object and adjunct material commonly follow the verb. Dependent clauses are regularly introduced by subordinators or complementizers (although, that, if, while) and relative clauses follow their head nouns. Non-finite -ing clauses and fronted prepositional/temporal adjuncts are frequent and often attach to the nearest clause rather than forming independent sentences.
